meta.title: Who really said "Do not wait; the time will never be just right. Start where you stand, and work with whatever tools you may have at your command, and better tools will be found as you go along"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Napoleon Hill wrote it, in Think and Grow Rich (1937), chapter 7, as cause of failure No. 8. But he punctuated it as two sentences, not one.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Do not wait; the time will never be just right. Start where you stand, and work with whatever tools you may have at your command, and better tools will be found as you go along'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Napoleon Hill — verified in the full text of Think and Grow Rich (1937), chapter 7. The circulating semicolon version is lightly repunctuated.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed word for word in the full text of Think and Grow Rich (1937), where it closes cause of failure No. 8, “Procrastination,” in Chapter 7, “Organized Planning.” Hill punctuated it as two sentences — “Do not wait. The time will never be ‘just right.’” — so the semicolon in the version that circulates is a later tidy-up, not his.

source.heading: Think and Grow Rich, Chapter 7

docMeta.dd: Chapter 7, “Organized Planning” — cause of failure No. 8, “Procrastination”
Two sentences: “Do not wait. The time will never be ‘just right.’”

source.excerpt: 8. PROCRASTINATION. This is one of the most common causes of failure. “Old Man Procrastination” stands within the shadow of every human being, waiting his opportunity to spoil one’s chances of success. Most of us go through life as failures, because we are waiting for the “time to be right” to start doing something worthwhile. Do not wait. The time will never be “just right.” Start where you stand, and work with whatever tools you may have at your command, and better tools will be found as you go along.
trail: The sentence is not a free-floating aphorism. It is the last line of item 8, “Procrastination,” in the list of major causes of failure that fills the back half of Chapter 7 of Think and Grow Rich ↗, where the scanned full text carries it word for word.
A second, independently uploaded scan of the book on the Internet Archive carries the identical wording, punctuation included — this copy ↗ — so the match is not an artefact of one bad OCR pass.
Wikiquote ↗ files the line under Think and Grow Rich too, though it heads that section 1938; Wikipedia ↗ gives the book’s release as 1937, by The Ralston Society.
Quote Investigator has no entry ↗ for this line. There is no rival origin story to weigh here — the book itself is the evidence.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the scanned full text at the Internet Archive. Printed page numbers vary between editions and reprints, so the chapter and the numbered item are the stable locator; Wikiquote’s entry cites p. 127 in whichever edition it used.

source.rightsNote: The date alone does not settle this one. Think and Grow Rich was first published in 1937 by The Ralston Society, so its U.S. term ran under the 1909 Act: 28 years from publication, extended only if a renewal was filed in the 28th year — 1965 here. A book of that vintage that was never renewed is in the public domain today, whichever later term-extension rule you apply. The renewal record for the 1937 first edition is contested: free full-text editions circulate on the claim that no renewal was filed, while the Napoleon Hill Foundation ↗, founded in 1963, still sells Hill’s books and courses and holds a registered trademark in the title ↗ — a trademark, note, not a copyright claim in the text. Until that renewal record is confirmed either way, quotle.info takes the conservative reading and treats the book as in copyright. The scans on the Internet Archive are not a rights determination either.

author.name: Napoleon Hill
author.heading: Who was Napoleon Hill?
author.metaLine: 1883–1970 · American self-help author · Think and Grow Rich (1937)
author.bio: Napoleon Hill was an American writer and lecturer whose Think and Grow Rich (1937) became one of the best-selling self-help books ever published. He built it around a claim that Andrew Carnegie personally commissioned him to distil the formula for success — a claim no historian has been able to corroborate. Wikipedia's article describes him as a self-help author, journalist, salesman and lecturer with a long record of criminal charges and fraud accusations, which is worth knowing before reading anything in his books as reportage.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The credit to Napoleon Hill is correct — but a large slice of the quote web files this line under George Herbert, an English poet who died three centuries before Hill wrote it. What else travels is a lightly repunctuated and sometimes mangled version of the real Hill sentence, usually cut loose from the paragraph that gives it its point.

items.why: AZQuotes ↗ files the sentence verbatim on its George Herbert page, BiblePortal ↗ runs it as a Herbert line under “Perseverance,” and BrainyQuote gives it a dedicated Herbert page — from which it spreads to school papers and poster prints. Herbert (1593–1633) died three hundred and four years before Think and Grow Rich was printed, and Wikiquote’s sourced Herbert page ↗ carries nothing of the kind. This is an aggregator-born credit, not a rival origin story.

Hill wrote two sentences, with his own quotation marks: “Do not wait. The time will never be ‘just right.’” The familiar “Do not wait; the time will never be just right” welds them into one and drops his quote marks around ‘just right.’ Same words, tidier punctuation — compare the book ↗.

items.who: Goodreads and the sites that copy it
items.why: The heavily reposted version reads “Do not wait: the time will never be ‘just right’. Start where you stand, and work whatever tools you may have at your command” — a colon instead of a full stop, and Hill’s “work with whatever tools” missing its preposition. It is also posted with no book named at all: see the listing ↗.

In the book the line is the payoff of a diagnosis, not a slogan. It follows “Most of us go through life as failures, because we are waiting for the ‘time to be right’ to start doing something worthwhile” — and the whole item is headed PROCRASTINATION, one of the causes of failure Hill lists in Chapter 7 ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is genuinely Hill’s, not George Herbert’s: it closes cause of failure No. 8, “Procrastination,” in Chapter 7 of Think and Grow Rich ↗ (1937) — punctuated by Hill as two sentences, not one.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: Think and Grow Rich came out in 1937, into a country still climbing out of the Depression, and it is mostly a book of metaphysics: thoughts are things, desire is a force, the subconscious can be dictated to. This sentence is the rare passage that asks you to believe nothing at all. It is a plain instruction about starting badly rather than not starting, and it survives on quote cards nearly ninety years later precisely because it works without the rest of the system.

Hill framed the whole book as a commission from Andrew Carnegie, who supposedly handed him the secret and asked him to spend twenty years proving it out. That origin story has not held up. Carnegie’s biographer David Nasaw told journalist Matt Novak he “found no evidence of any sort that Carnegie and Hill ever met.” The advice in item 8 is really Hill’s; the pedigree he claimed for it is another matter.
detailsBody: Hill’s own Author’s Preface opens the Carnegie claim: the secret “was brought to my attention by Andrew Carnegie, more than a quarter of a century ago,” who then asked whether Hill would spend twenty years or more preparing to take it to the world. Nothing in the surviving record supports the meeting.

Wikipedia’s article on Hill ↗ goes further, describing him as a con man alongside author and lecturer, and cataloguing mail-fraud and blue-sky-law charges across his career. None of that touches whether he wrote this sentence — he did — but it is the reason to read his books as rhetoric rather than record.

sourcesVerified.claim: The scanned full text of Think and Grow Rich in this Internet Archive item contains, verbatim in Chapter 7 as item 8 'PROCRASTINATION': 'Do not wait. The time will never be "just right." Start where you stand, and work with whatever tools you may have at your command, and better tools will be found as you go along.'
A second, independently uploaded Internet Archive scan of Think and Grow Rich carries the identical sentence with identical punctuation in the same numbered item.
Wikiquote's Napoleon Hill page lists this line under a section headed 'Think and Grow Rich (1938)', citing p. 127, and also carries the fuller 'Most of us go through life as failures...' form.
Wikipedia states Think and Grow Rich was released in 1937 by The Ralston Society.

Wikipedia gives Napoleon Hill's dates as 26 October 1883 – 8 November 1970, describes him as an American self-help author, con man, journalist, salesman and lecturer, notes the Napoleon Hill Foundation was founded in 1963 and still sells his books and courses, and records that historians doubt his claim to have met Andrew Carnegie.
Matt Novak's Gizmodo article (6 December 2016) quotes Carnegie biographer David Nasaw saying he 'found no evidence of any sort that Carnegie and Hill ever met.'

Goodreads carries the line attributed to Napoleon Hill with no book cited, worded 'Do not wait: the time will never be "just right". Start where you stand, and work whatever tools you may have at your command and better tools will be found as you go along.'
Quote Investigator has no article on this quotation; a site search for 'time will never be just right' returns 'Nothing Found'.

AZQuotes carries the line verbatim on a George Herbert quote page: 'Do not wait; the time will never be "just right." Start where you stand, and work with whatever tools you may have at your command, and better tools will be found as you go along.' — attributed to George Herbert.
BiblePortal files the same sentence under George Herbert, in its 'Perseverance' topic.

Wikiquote's sourced George Herbert page contains no line beginning 'Do not wait' or 'Start where you stand' — its quotations come from The Temple (1633), Herbert's Remains (1652) and Jacula Prudentum (1651).

The Napoleon Hill Foundation's own 'Trademarks & Copyrights' page lists 'Think and Grow Rich®' among its registered trademarks and describes challenging unauthorized uses of that trademark; it asserts no copyright in the 1937 text.
